strengths: The paper tackles an important problem: improving end-to-end autonomous driving in long-tail scenarios by combining VLM-based scene understanding, diffusion trajectory generation, and simulator-assisted RL.
The proposed three-stage pipeline is coherent and technically plausible, with a clear motivation for replacing autoregressive textual trajectory prediction with a continuous diffusion planner.
The NAVSIM results are strong, reporting a new PDMS of 89.6 and outperforming several vision-only and sensor-fusion baselines, including recent diffusion-based methods.

The ablation studies are useful: driving-domain QA pretraining, the diffusion planner, and RL fine-tuning each contribute measurable gains, with the largest gains coming from domain pretraining and RL.
The supplementary material provides helpful implementation details, dataset processing descriptions, hyperparameters, and extended NAVSIM metrics.
weaknesses: The evaluation is too narrow for the strength of the claims. Nearly all evidence comes from NAVSIM, a small non-reactive benchmark, yet the paper makes broad claims about real-world viability, safety, and long-tail generalization.

The RL stage appears to optimize the same simulator metrics used for evaluation, raising concerns about benchmark overfitting. It is unclear whether hyperparameters and ablations were selected using the test split, which would further weaken the validity of the reported gains.

Novelty is moderate rather than strong. The method combines existing components: InternVL-style driving adaptation, diffusion planning, and GRPO-like RL fine-tuning. The paper does not sufficiently distinguish its technical contribution from closely related recent work such as DiffusionDrive, AlphaDrive, and VLM-action models.

The comparison may be unfair or incomplete because ReCogDrive uses a very large 8B VLM and a 3.1M QA corpus, while many baselines use much smaller models or different sensor/data regimes. Compute, data scale, and latency are not normalized or deeply analyzed.

Reproducibility is limited. The large curated QA dataset, automatic annotation pipeline, filtering criteria, prompts, and generated NAVSIM QA annotations are central to the method but not specified in enough detail to reproduce the results confidently.

The paper lacks evaluation on other autonomous driving benchmarks, interactive closed-loop simulators, held-out long-tail subsets, or real-world deployment settings. This is especially problematic given the safety-critical domain.

The safety and broader-impact discussion is quite superficial. The paper emphasizes reduced collision risk but does not analyze failure modes, hallucinated explanations, distribution shift, latency, or risks from deploying VLM-based planners in autonomous driving.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence supports, such as confirming scaling laws, injecting generalized cognition, and demonstrating real-world viability. The reported experiments support benchmark improvement, but not these broader conclusions.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: improving end-to-end autonomous driving in long-tail scenarios using VLM representations, continuous trajectory decoding, and simulator feedback.
The proposed system is conceptually coherent: driving-domain VLM adaptation, a diffusion trajectory planner, and RL fine-tuning are reasonable components for this task.
Reported NAVSIM results are strong, with a PDMS of 89.6 and ablations suggesting gains from driving QA pretraining, diffusion planning, and RL fine-tuning.
The supplement provides useful implementation details, dataset composition, hyperparameters, and some extended NAVSIM metrics.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited. The paper mostly combines existing ingredients: InternVL-style VLM fine-tuning, diffusion policy/planning, and GRPO/REINFORCE-style simulator optimization. The claimed contribution is more system integration than a clearly new technical advance.

The evaluation is too narrow for the strength of the claims. Results are almost entirely on NAVSIM, a non-reactive simulator with only 136 navtest scenes, yet the paper claims safer, human-like behavior and real-world viability. There is no evaluation in an interactive closed-loop simulator, no real-world data test, and no robustness or long-tail breakdown.

The RL setup risks optimizing directly to the benchmark metric rather than demonstrating generalizable driving ability. PDMS is used as the reward and also as the main evaluation metric, and the paper does not convincingly rule out metric overfitting or show transfer to different reward definitions, datasets, or simulators.

Baselines and comparisons are not fully convincing. The VLM baselines appear weak and narrowly reproduced, while several closely related recent VLM/RL driving systems are only discussed in related work rather than compared experimentally. Compute and input-modality differences also make some comparisons hard to interpret.

The ablation evidence is incomplete. The diffusion planner alone adds only 0.6 PDMS after driving pretraining, and the largest gain comes from RL on the same simulator metric. There are no ablations on VLM freezing, spatial pooling choices, number of sampled trajectories, reward components, dataset leakage, or statistical variance across seeds.

Reproducibility is weak for a large-scale system. The method depends on 3.1M curated QA pairs, Qwen2.5-VL relabeling/filtering, NAVSIM-specific auto-annotations, and 32 H20 GPUs, but the paper does not provide enough detail to independently reconstruct the data or training pipeline, nor does it mention code/model/data release.

The technical description of the RL objective is shallow. It assigns a trajectory-level PDMS reward across the diffusion denoising chain, uses group-normalized advantages, and adds a BC term, but gives little analysis of variance, stability, KL control, reward sparsity, or why this is sound for safety-critical planning.

The paper overclaims interpretability and cognition. Generated descriptions and reasoning traces are shown qualitatively, but there is no quantitative evaluation that the language outputs are faithful to the planner’s decision process or causally useful for safety.

The system uses only front-view imagery despite autonomous driving requiring multi-camera temporal understanding; the authors acknowledge this limitation, but it undercuts the claimed real-world relevance.

Safety and broader impacts are underdeveloped. For an autonomous driving paper, the ethical and deployment discussion is too brief, with no serious treatment of failure modes, hallucination risks, validation requirements, or misuse of benchmark-optimized policies.

strengths: Clear and timely problem: improving long-tail autonomous driving by combining VLM-based scene understanding with continuous trajectory generation and simulator-based policy improvement is relevant and significant.

The system design is coherent: driving-domain VLM adaptation, a diffusion planner to bridge language representations and continuous control, and RL fine-tuning form a plausible pipeline with well-motivated components.

Empirical results on NAVSIM/NA VSIM are strong: the method reports a new state of the art PDMS of 89.6 and outperforms both VLM baselines and several strong non-VLM planners, including methods using LiDAR.
Ablations are useful and support the main architectural claims: driving QA pretraining, the diffusion planner, and RL fine-tuning each improve performance, with RL giving a substantial final gain.
The supplementary material provides meaningful implementation detail, dataset construction description, hyperparameters, extended metrics, limitations, and qualitative examples.
weaknesses: The evaluation is concentrated on a single non-reactive simulator benchmark. This weakens claims about real-world viability, long-tail robustness, and closed-loop safety, especially because the RL reward is derived from the same simulator family used for evaluation.

Novelty is solid but not clearly exceptional: the paper combines several recent trends, including VLM driving models, diffusion policy/planning, and GRPO-style RL, but the conceptual advance over adjacent work is incremental rather than groundbreaking.

The contribution of the VLM cognition itself is not deeply isolated. The paper does not convincingly test whether language reasoning, scene descriptions, or textual intermediate outputs are causally necessary beyond serving as learned visual features.

Reproducibility may be challenging: the approach uses a large 3.1M QA corpus, automatic re-annotation/filtering by proprietary or large external VLMs, and 32 H20 GPUs, while release details for data, code, and annotations are unclear.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence, particularly regarding human-like behavior, rare/long-tail generalization, and safety. The paper would benefit from scenario-stratified evaluations, failure analysis, uncertainty analysis, and comparison on additional planning datasets or reactive simulators.

Practical deployment issues are underexplored. The authors acknowledge high inference latency and limited multi-camera/video handling, but the main experiments do not quantify latency, memory, or robustness under sensor/domain shifts.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: combining VLM-based driving cognition with continuous trajectory planning for end-to-end autonomous driving.
The proposed system is reasonably well motivated: text-form trajectory generation has clear practical drawbacks, and the diffusion planner is a natural way to address continuous action generation.
Empirical results are strong on the reported benchmarks, including state-of-the-art PDMS on NA VSIM and competitive closed-loop performance on Bench2Drive.
The paper includes useful ablations over driving pretraining, diffusion planning, reinforcement learning, trajectory generation variants, BC loss weight, noise clipping, and discount factor.

The method is described with enough architectural and training detail to understand the overall pipeline, and the appendix provides additional hyperparameters, qualitative examples, limitations, and failure cases.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is mostly an integration of existing ingredients: InternVL-style VLMs, hierarchical VQA data generation, DiT/diffusion planning, and GRPO-like reinforcement learning. The paper would benefit from a clearer distinction between genuinely new algorithmic contributions and engineering composition.

The role of the VLM cognition is not fully convincing. Table 10 shows that adding high-level commands or chain-of-thought does not improve planning, suggesting the main gains may come from the diffusion planner and simulator RL rather than explicit cognitive reasoning.

The RL stage optimizes with NA VSIM simulator feedback and is evaluated heavily on NA VSIM-style metrics, raising concerns about benchmark-specific reward overfitting. More evidence on held-out domains or substantially different scenarios would strengthen the safety/generalization claims.

The data pipeline is large but somewhat opaque. Automatic annotation, refinement, and quality scoring depend on Qwen2.5-VL, yet prompts, filtering calibration, error rates, and possible annotation bias are not analyzed in depth.

Evaluation breadth is good but not fully decisive. NA VSIM navtest has only 136 evaluation scenes, Bench2Drive has low absolute success rate despite being best among baselines, and there is no real-vehicle or high-fidelity out-of-distribution validation.

Some claims are overstated. For example, the paper claims strong reliability and safety, but qualitative failure cases include aggressive driving, weak multi-view perception, and unsafe following distance; Bench2Drive also shows weak comfort and mixed multi-ability performance.

Reproducibility is incomplete from the manuscript alone: the abstract appears to leave the code/model link blank, and training requires very large-scale data, 32 H20 GPUs, proprietary/generated annotations, and potentially unavailable benchmark-specific pipelines.

The broader impacts section is too shallow for autonomous driving. It does not seriously discuss deployment risks, simulator-to-real gaps, failure monitoring, liability, or safeguards for safety-critical use.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: improving end-to-end autonomous driving by combining VLM representations with continuous trajectory generation rather than text-formatted action outputs.

The reported NAVSIM and Bench2Drive numbers are strong, and the paper includes several useful ablations on driving pretraining, diffusion planning, RL fine-tuning, inference speed, and some RL hyperparameters.

The diffusion-planner direction is practically motivated: avoiding autoregressive text decoding for trajectories plausibly improves latency, removes parsing failures, and better matches the continuous action space.
weaknesses: The central claim that cognitive VLM reasoning guides planning is not convincingly supported. The appendix shows that trajectory-only prediction matches or slightly outperforms high-level command and CoT guidance, making the VLM appear closer to a feature extractor than a demonstrated reasoning component.

Novelty is limited relative to existing VLM-driving, diffusion-policy, and RL fine-tuning work. The proposed DiffGRPO is essentially a simple REINFORCE-style objective over diffusion-chain likelihoods with group-normalized rewards and a BC term; the paper does not establish a substantial algorithmic advance over prior diffusion policy optimization or GRPO-like driving work.

Evaluation is too narrow for the strength of the safety and SOTA claims. NAVSIM navtest has only 136 evaluation scenes, no confidence intervals or multi-seed variance are reported, and the main RL reward substantially overlaps with the reported NAVSIM metric, raising concerns about benchmark-specific optimization.

The Bench2Drive results are mixed despite the positive framing: success is only 45.45%, comfort is much worse than many baselines, and multi-ability mean is only marginally best/competitive, which weakens claims of robust closed-loop reliability.

The data pipeline is underspecified and not well validated. Large-scale QA generation, refinement, and quality scoring rely heavily on Qwen2.5-VL, but the paper provides little evidence that these annotations are correct, diverse, or free of systematic errors; automated self-filtering is not a substitute for human or task-level validation in a safety-critical domain.

Reproducibility is weak. The abstract advertises code/model availability but the link is blank in the manuscript; the training requires large proprietary/generated datasets, Qwen2.5-VL-72B annotation, and 32 GPUs, with insufficient detail to reproduce the data construction and RL environment.

There are concerning inconsistencies and presentation issues: the reported BC loss weight differs between the best ablation and hyperparameter table, the noise clipping value differs between text and table, and Table 7 contains a malformed value. These reduce confidence in experimental care.

The safety and broader-impact discussion is superficial for autonomous driving. The paper claims reduced collision risk and real-world relevance but only evaluates in simulation/benchmarks and does not address deployment risks, failure severity, distribution shift, or validation requirements for safety-critical use.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem in end-to-end autonomous driving: combining the semantic/cognitive strengths of VLMs with continuous, feasible trajectory generation rather than relying on brittle text-formatted actions.

The proposed ReCogDrive framework is coherent and practically motivated, with a clear three-stage recipe: driving-oriented VLM pretraining, cognition-guided diffusion planning, and simulator-based reinforcement learning via DiffGRPO.

The empirical results are strong. The method reports state-of-the-art performance on NA VSIM and competitive-to-leading results on Bench2Drive, including improvements over both vision-only and camera+LiDAR baselines while using camera input.

The ablation studies support the main design choices: driving pretraining, diffusion planning, and DiffGRPO each contribute measurable gains, and the trajectory-generation comparison demonstrates both accuracy and latency benefits over plain-text trajectory prediction.

The paper includes useful supplementary analysis, including extended NA VSIM metrics, VQA/DriveBench evaluations, hyperparameter studies, qualitative examples, and failure cases, which makes the submission more complete than a narrow benchmark paper.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is moderate rather than exceptional. Much of the method combines existing ingredients: VLM finetuning, diffusion planners, GRPO-style policy optimization, and simulator rewards. The contribution is mainly a well-engineered integration with strong empirical validation.

The RL stage optimizes a simulator-derived PDMS-style reward and is then evaluated heavily on NA VSIM/related metrics, raising concern that part of the improvement may be benchmark/reward specialization rather than broad driving robustness.

The strongest NA VSIM evaluation uses only 136 evaluation scenes, and the paper would be more convincing with stronger statistical analysis, variance over seeds, or additional held-out closed-loop settings beyond the reported benchmarks.

The role of the VLM in final planning is somewhat weakened by the authors’ own analysis: high-level command and CoT guidance do not improve performance, suggesting the planner may benefit more from learned features and data scale than from explicit cognitive reasoning.

The data pipeline relies on large-scale automatically generated QA annotations from strong VLMs, but annotation quality, possible biases, and overlap/contamination risks across driving VQA resources and evaluation tasks are not fully characterized.

Reproducibility remains somewhat limited by the scale of training, dependence on large VLMs and generated datasets, extensive compute requirements, and an apparently incomplete code/model link in the manuscript text.
